Testimony in Opposition: LD 837, An Act to Require the Office of the Public Advocate to Implement the State's Climate Action Plan
Greetings Senator Lawrence, Representative Sachs, and honorable members of the Joint Standing Committee on Energy, Utilities and Technology. My name is Alf Anderson, and I am an Associate State Director for Advocacy and Outreach for AARP Maine. AARP is a non-profit, non-partisan social mission organization with more than 200,000 members across the state. We work on a range of energy issues at the state level. The core principles we approach this work with include affordability, reliability, and accountability.
I'm here today to testify in opposition to LD 837. The purpose of this bill is to add a mandate to the statutes governing the Office of Public Advocate to require that office to "implement the state climate action pursuant to Title 38, section 577." AARP Maine opposes this bill for the following reasons.
First, the Office of Public Advocate does not "implement" the provisions of laws in Title 38, section 577. That provision of Maine law is part of the laws governing the Department of Environmental Protection and the Maine Climate Council. The Office of Public Advocate has no jurisdiction over these entities and no independent role in the implementation of the statutory duties of these agencies.
Second, the primary role of the Public Advocate is to represent ratepayers in proceedings before the Maine Public Utilities Commission. The Office of Public Advocate is charged as follows:
35-A MRSA Sec. 1702 (10): Independent representation of the interests of the using and consuming public. The Public Advocate, when taking a position on any matter in any proceeding or forum pursuant to the Public Advocate's authority under this chapter, shall exercise independent judgment to ensure the position:
A. Is consistent with the priorities established in section 1702-A and the requirements of this chapter; and [PL 2011, c. 79, �2 (NEW).] B. Promotes stabilization and lowering of prices paid by those members of the using and consuming public whose interests the Public Advocate is representing.
The priorities set forth in Section 1702-A require the OPA to focus on the needs of low-income

residential consumers, residential consumers, small business consumers, and other consumers that the Advocate finds are not properly represented in proceedings before the PUC. This statutory mandate should not be changed. Rather, it is the duty of the Public Advocate to have the independent voice of ratepayers to focus on the affordability and reasonableness of essential utility service. This mandate does not conflict with or require any changes to take into account the obligations of other state agencies to implement Maine's Climate Plan. The role of the OPA has been, and should continue to be, to act as a watchdog ensuring that utility companies do not unfairly increase rates or implement practices that harm consumers. Their staff bring specialized knowledge and expertise to ensure that decisions are based on accurate data and that consumers' voices are heard. They help level the playing field by providing an independent perspective and counterbalancing the influence of the large utilities. Requiring the OPA to implement the state's Climate Action Plan (presumably without additional funding) would detract from their important role. I urge you to vote no on LD 837 and allow the Office of the Public Advocate to continue to act as the voice of Maine's utilities customers. Thank you for the opportunity to provide our views on this important bill. If I can answer any questions or provide any further information, you can reach me at aanderson@aarp.org or 207.330.1147. Alf Anderson Associate State Director, Advocacy and Outreach AARP Maine

Joint Committee on Energy, Utilities and Technology Andrew Blunt, Legislative and Political Strategist, Sierra Club Maine March 18, 2025 Testimony in Support of L.D. 837: An Act to Require the Office of the Public Advocate to Implement the State's Climate Action Plan

Senator Lawrence, Representative Sachs, and members of the Joint Committee On Energy, Utilities and Technology,

My name is Andrew Blunt, and I write on behalf of Sierra Club Maine, representing over 22,000 supporters and members statewide. Founded in 1892, Sierra Club is one of our nation's oldest and largest environmental organizations. We work diligently to amplify the power of our 3.8 million members nationwide as we work towards combating climate change and promoting a just and sustainable economy.

Title 38, Section 577, the concerned section, is concerned with the creation of the State's Climate Action Plan but it does not appear to otherwise alter the duties or authority of those actors. The Public Advocate was not originally included in the array of groups convened for this purpose, and this bill simply directs the Advocate to use his or her existing authorities to further the climate action plan. The duties of the Advocate are found in Title 35-A, Chapter 17 of Maine's statutes.

This bill does not expressly override those duties and a rule of statutory interpretation is that "preemption is not to be implied" but that newer statutes are meant to be read as supporting the existing laws if at all possible. So, as our testimony points out, this short bill should be read to guide the Advocate in seeing and factoring in the long term costs of climate change as one of the costs to be minimized as we provide utility services to the people and especially the low-income people and small businesses of Maine as the existing law emphasizes.

Harmonizing the duties of the Public Advocate, an office that has historically been solely focused on reducing costs for consumers, with the work of the Maine Climate Council is a common-sense solution to ensure that the Public Advocate works for the long-term benefit of the consumers, not just the short term. Addressing climate change is a complex, layered task. By aligning the Office of the Public Advocate with the needs of the Maine Climate Council, we can continue working to ensure that all state offices engaged in conversation about energy policy and electricity are rowing together to respond to climate change in a coordinated fashion.

The Public Advocate's work is highly relevant to many of the goals of Maine's existing climate action plan, "Maine Won't Wait." Strategy C, "Transition to Clean Energy," strikes at the core of the Public Advocates work, particularly efforts to build new transmission and distribution infrastructure. This grid buildout will certainly come with a cost, and while it is imperative that these costs are

 minimized for ratepayers, especially low-income ratepayers, it is also crucial that the Public Advocate does not work at odds with the buildout and modernization of our electric grid.
In cases where ratepayer interests hold complex relationships with climate initiatives, it is important that the Public Advocate considers climate change in their work as they build advocacy positions for their ratepayers. Too often, the short term dollars and cents reflected on electricity bills do not tell the story of the broader, social costs of climate change.
We urge the Committee to continue building alignment throughout state agencies on climate change and vote "ought to pass" on L.D. 837.
Sincerely,
Andrew Blunt Sierra Club Maine Legislative and Political Strategist

LD 837 An Act to Require the Office of the Public Advocate to Implement the State's Climate Action Plan Testimony in Support March 18, 2025
Senator Lawrence, Representative Sachs, and members of the Committee on Energy, Utilities and Technology, my name is Hannah Pingree, and I am the Director of the Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future (GOPIF), and co-chair of the Maine Climate Council.
I am pleased to submit testimony in support of LD 837, An Act to Require the Office of the Public Advocate to Implement the state's climate action plan. I think the goal of Senator Lawrence's legislation is important, and it speaks to the importance of multiple state agencies supporting the goals of the state's climate action plan and bringing their expertise to the table to ensure equitable, affordable implementation. Further, we also share a suggested concept for amendment consideration, that would bring the Public Advocate's statute into line with the Public Utilities Commission.
On November 21, 2024 the Maine Climate Council released the state's updated four-year action plan, Maine Won't Wait (PDF). The updated plan builds on the state's success in fighting climate change and recommends commonsense strategies to advance the state's work in reducing greenhouse gas emissions, achieving carbon neutrality, and increase Maine's resilience to the impacts of increasing extreme storm events. The past two years have thrown into sharp relief the impact of climate-driven weather events in Maine communities. Persistent warming trends on land and at sea are generating more frequent and damaging storms, rising seas, flooding, and drought, all of which threaten the lives of Maine's people, their livelihoods in Maine's heritage industries, and our economy and environment.
By law, Maine must reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 45 percent by 2030 and by at least 80 percent by 2050. The Maine Department of Environmental Protection (DEP), in consultation with the Maine Climate Council, is responsible for evaluating the state's progress toward meeting the greenhouse gas reductions specified in section 576A and progress toward implementing the climate action plan in section 577 and is required to adopt rules to ensure the state's progress.
Given the important role of energy policy in accomplishing the state's climate goals, as well the increasing impacts of extreme storm events on our state's electricity grid reliability and rate payers, it is an important time for the Public Advocate to be engaged in these issues.
To that end, respectfully, I'd like to offer some suggested language for the sponsor's and committee's consideration that would align the Public Advocate's statute with the Public Utilities Commission's statute. The Public Utilities Commission statute, PL 2021, c. 279, �1 and PL 2021, c. 279, �2, requires the commission to consider the state's greenhouse gas reduction goals when making policy. To match the Commission's language, the Public Advocate statute could include the following in requirements:
In executing the duties and responsibilities under this Title, the Public Advocate, while representing the using and consuming public in matters within the jurisdiction of the

Testimony in Opposition to LD 837: "An Act to Require the Office of the Public Advocate to Implement
the State's Climate Action Plan"
Senator Lawrence, Representative Sachs, and the distinguished members of the Committee On Energy, Utilities and Technology, my name is Harris Van Pate, and I serve as policy analyst for Maine Policy Institute. Maine Policy is a free market think tank, a nonpartisan, non-profit organization that advocates for individual liberty and economic freedom in Maine. Thank you for the opportunity to testify in opposition to LD 837, which would require the Office of the Public Advocate (OPA) to implement the state's Climate Action Plan.
Maine Policy firmly believes in limited government, free-market solutions, and policies that put Mainers first. Unfortunately, LD 837 undermines the OPA's fundamental mission of protecting ratepayers and risks further entrenching costly and unreliable energy policies that burden Maine households and businesses.
Undermining the Independence of the Public Advocate
The OPA serves as an independent watchdog for Maine's energy consumers. As outlined in 35-A M.R.S. �1702, the Public Advocate's primary duty is "to represent the using and consuming public" in proceedings before the Public Utilities Commission (PUC) and certain other regulatory bodies.1 This role requires an impartial approach to ensure that ratepayer interests are prioritized over political or ideological considerations, which is why 35-A M.R.S. �1702.10 clarifies that the Public Advocate "shall exercise independent judgment" when taking positions on any proceeding. Subsection B clarifies that these positions must promote stabilizing and lowering energy prices for the consuming public.
Forcing the OPA to implement the Climate Action Plan would compromise its independence and shift its focus from advocating for affordable, reliable energy to advancing a climate policy agenda that imposes substantial costs on Maine consumers. Ratepayers--particularly those in rural and low-income communities--should not bear the financial burden of policies prioritizing broad climate goals over affordability and energy reliability.
The Cost Burden of Maine's Climate Action Plan
Implementing the Climate Action Plan will have significant cost implications for Maine ratepayers.2 A recent policy review found that mandates for renewable energy from New
1 https://legislature.maine.gov/statutes/35-a/title35-Asec1702.html 2 https://mainepolicy.org/climate-council-should-learn-from-ev-debacle-in-developing-maines-next-climate-plan/

England states and electric vehicle (EV) adoption would result in higher electricity prices, reduced grid reliability, and increased dependence on out-of-state energy sources.3
Maine already has some of the highest electricity rates in the nation, currently the fifth highest KwH price for residential consumers and eighth highest for business rates.4 These prices are in part due to aggressive renewable energy mandates and costly subsidies for solar and wind power.5 Furthermore, many of these costs would not even be presented to the public without our current independent public advocate.6
Additionally, LD 837 risks exposing the state to costly legal battles. Environmental groups such as the Sierra Club have sued Maine in federal court for its decision not to implement a controversial EV mandate.7 Expanding the OPA's duties to include climate policy implementation increases the likelihood of additional litigation if these groups are not happy with the degree to which these policies are pursued, diverting resources from its core mission of advocating for ratepayers.
Energy Reliability and the Risks of Over-Reliance on Renewables
Maine's growing investment in intermittent renewable energy--while failing to support baseload power sources like natural gas and nuclear adequately--has contributed to regional energy instability and higher costs. As noted in Maine Policy's research, the overreliance on wind and solar without appropriate backup generation capacity has led to spiking electricity prices and increased reliance on imported power during peak demand periods.
With rising importation and storage costs and the need to overbuild when focusing on these non-dispatchable energy sources, a robust, diversified energy strategy, including natural gas, nuclear, and emerging technologies, is essential to maintaining affordability and reliability.8 However, Maine's Climate Action Plan ignores these realities, favoring a politically driven decarbonization strategy that will leave ratepayers vulnerable to energy shortages and price volatility.

Conclusion
The Office of the Public Advocate must focus on its statutory role--protecting ratepayers and ensuring affordable, reliable energy. LD 837 would fundamentally alter this mission, forcing the OPA to implement policies that increase costs and reduce energy reliability while exposing the state to unnecessary legal risks.
Maine cannot afford to jeopardize the independence of the Public Advocate in service of an energy agenda that prioritizes political goals over consumer welfare. For these reasons, we strongly urge the committee to reject LD 837. Thank you for your time and consideration.

The Nature Conservancy (TNC) is a nonprofit conservation organization dedicated to conserving
the lands and waters on which all life depends. Guided by science, we create innovative, on-the-
ground solutions to our world's toughest challenges so that both nature and people can thrive.
We work in more than 70 countries, and we use a collaborative approach that engages local
communities, governments, the private sector, and other partners.

The Nature Conservancy strongly supports this bill for three key reasons:

1. Cost savings and economic efficiency are key considerations of the state Climate Action Plan and align well with the mission of the Maine Public Advocate.

35-A M.R.S. � 1702(A) clarifies that it is the "intent of the Legislature that the resources of the
Public Advocate be devoted to the maximum extent possible to ensuring adequate representation of the interests of those consumers whose interests would otherwise be
inadequately represented" before the PUC. While the statute goes on to rank in order of priority low-income customers, residential customers, etc. the law stipulates that this subsection "does not require the Public Advocate to represent interests of one group if the Public Advocate determines that such representation is adverse to the overall interests of the using and
consuming public/'1

TNC believes that failing to consider the impacts of climate change by advocating for lower
upfront costs above all else is adverse to the overall interests ofthe using and consuming public. Moreso, low-income Mainers are the most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change and those with the highest energy burdens have the most to gain by implementing energy efficiency measures outlined in the Climate Action Plan (CAP).
There are several strategies in the 2024 Maine Won't Wait plan that outline "cost--effective" options to address climate change including but not limited to: Strategy B: Modernize Maine's
Buildings: Energy Efficient, Smart, and Cost-Effective Homes and Businesses; Strategy C: Transition to Clean Energy, which recognizes the "key role of clean energy in bringing down the

cost of electricity for Maine people" while also investing in technology to increase efficiency and resiliency with demand management technology; and Strategy D, focused on creating jobs and growing Maine's Economy through Climate Action?

To illustrate a real-life example, a recent study by the American Council for an Energy-Efficient
Economy found that in Maine, "switching to heat pumps will cut monthly utility bills over the course of a year."3 Maine exceeded our goal of installing 100,000 heat pumps statewide, and then set a more ambitious target of installing 275,000 heat pumps by 2027. If the OPA is to "implement the state climate action plan" , as LD 837 requires, we could expect the OPA to represent the ratepayer before the PUC by advocating for things such as resiliency measures and
increased electrification.

2. Maine ratepayers understand the importance of addressing climate change by transitioning to renewable energy and implementing energy efficiency measures.
A recent poll conducted by TNC indicates that most Mainers are worried about the high cost of electricity, but they also understand the importance of addressing climate change. 71% of Maine
voters found the cost of electricity to be an extremely serious or very serious concern, but at the
same time a majority indicated their understanding that it will be more costly for Maine if we do
not act to address climate change. This demonstrates that the people of Maine believe it to be in their best interest to implement the recommendations from the CAP.

3. Not asking the Public Advocate to implement the Climate Action Plan is a missed opportunity that will ultimately harm Maine ratepayers.

The Maine Climate Council, which TNC Maine's state director, Kate Dempsey was a member of,
found that inaction to address climate change will cost Maine substantially more, and will accelerate over time, compared to the costs incurred by implementing the plan.` The 2024 Climate Action Plan references a 2020 Maine Climate Council report, The Cost of Doing Nothing, which found that, "Maine and its people face economic, ecosystem, and public health impacts if the state does not take action to prevent and prepare for climate change."5

Several of our staff scientists at TNC Maine were involved in working groups to help develop the

strategies and actions outlined in Maine Won't Wait, and we believe the recommendations in

the report reflect tangible, realistic solutions to addressing emissions while benefiting our

communities and protecting our natural environment.

10037864:
Testimony in Support of LD 837, An Act to Require the Office of the Public Advocate to Implement
the State's Climate Action Plan
To the Joint Committee on Energy, Utilities and Technology by Rebecca Schultz
Senior Advocate for Climate and Clean Energy March 18, 2025
Senator Lawrence, Representative Sachs, members of the Energy, Utilities and Technology Committee, my name is Rebecca Schultz, and I am a Senior Advocate for Climate and Clean Energy with the Natural Resources Council of Maine (NRCM). NRCM is a nonpartisan membership organization that has been working for more than 65 years to protect, restore, and conserve Maine's environment, now and for future generations.
On behalf of our nearly 24,000 members and supporters, NRCM testifies in support of LD 837, An Act to Require the Office of the Public Advocate to Implement the State's Climate Action Plan.
LD 837 proposes to modify the Public Advocate's governing charter to include the state's Climate Action Plan, pursuant to Title 38, section 577, among the duties of the Office.
The climate change crisis affects all of us and requires responses across the economy and across the government. LD 837 amounts to a good-housekeeping update to ensure continuity in an "all of government" approach to addressing climate change.
The Public Advocate plays a critical role at the Public Utilities Commission, representing the interests of Maine families and businesses. Those interests increasingly reside in the complex interplay of ratepayer costs and benefits across short- and long-term planning horizons, where upfront costs in shifting away from expensive, polluting fossil fuels will yield stable, affordable savings over the long-term.
Securing a homegrown supply of renewable energy and switching to efficient electric technologies in the transportation and heating sectors is the key to both overcoming our dependence on fossil fuels and providing a pathway to affordable, reliable energy for the state of Maine.
1

Navigating and advocating for Maine consumers throughout the state's transition to clean energy must be central to the work of the Public Advocate. And that's what this bill intends to make clear. In 2021, the 130th Legislature passed and the Governor signed LD 1682.1 That law established climate change requirements for the Public Utilities Commission and expanded the agency's statement of purpose to include reducing greenhouse gas emissions to levels set forth in Title 38, section 576-A.2 LD 837 can be understood as a companion bill to LD 1682, to bring the duties and responsibilities of the Public Advocate into alignment with the state's priority of addressing climate change. Acknowledging that the Office of the Public Advocate does not have direct implementation authority over most aspects of the state's Climate Action Plan, we would recommend friendly amendments to the bill to more appropriately reflect the nature of the role of the Office in advancing the state's climate and clean energy requirements. These minor modifications aside, we strongly support what we understand to be the sponsor's intention. We urge the Committee to vote Ought to Pass on LD 837. I would be happy to answer any questions that the Committee has and be available for work session. Thank you.
